opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, singular learning theory is fundamentally a theory of how the structure of the training data and the architecture get imprinted onto the geometry of the loss landscape, and then how that geometry shapes what the model actually learns. That turns out to be relevant to both evaluation and interpretability in some fairly concrete ways.

On the interpretability side, the key object is the local learning coefficient. You can think of it as a measure of the effective complexity of a model at a particular point in parameter space, or how degenerate the loss landscape is around the solution the model has found. What's nice is that it's something we can actually estimate at scale using sampling methods like SGLD. When you track the learning coefficient over the course of training, you find that development isn't smooth. There are distinct stages, and the transitions between them often line up with the model acquiring some new structure: in small language models, for example, things like learning bigram statistics, then forming induction heads, and so on. So SLT gives you a principled way to find the moments where something interesting is happening in a model's development, without having to know in advance what you're looking for.

We've also been pushing toward more refined versions, where you restrict the measurement to particular components, like individual attention heads, or to particular slices of data. That starts to look like a tool for attributing structure: which parts of the model are specializing to which parts of the distribution. The broader vision is something like a spectroscopy for neural networks, where you probe the model's response to perturbations of the weights and the data, and read off the internal structure from that.

On the evaluation side, I think the connection is about moving from behavioral snapshots toward understanding generalization. Benchmarks tell you what a model does on a fixed set of inputs. But what we really care about, especially for safety, is how the model will behave off-distribution, and that's ultimately a question about what algorithm or structure the model has internalized. SLT is, at its core, a theory of generalization for exactly the kinds of degenerate models we're training. So the hope is that geometric quantities can tell us things like whether a model has learned a general solution or a memorizing one, or flag when fine-tuning has introduced some new structure that a behavioral eval might miss.

I want to be honest that a lot of this is still early. The theory makes clean statements in the Bayesian setting, and there's real work involved in connecting that to models trained with SGD, and in making the estimators reliable at frontier scale. But the reason I'm excited is that it's one of the few approaches that tries to connect data, geometry, and learned structure in a single mathematical framework. If we want alignment to look more like an engineering discipline, with principled ways of measuring and eventually steering what models learn, I think we need a theory of that kind, and SLT is my best bet for where it comes from.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, singular learning theory is fundamentally a theory of how the geometry of the loss landscape shapes what a neural network ends up learning. And the key insight is that neural networks aren't like the simple models you see in classical statistics. They're singular, in the sense that the map from parameters to functions is degenerate. Many different parameter settings compute the same function, and the loss landscape has these valleys and ridges rather than nice isolated minima. Classical learning theory basically assumes that away, and SLT takes it seriously.

So why does that matter for interpretability and evaluations? I'd say there are a few threads.

The first is that SLT gives you a principled measure of complexity. There's this quantity called the local learning coefficient, which you can think of as an effective dimensionality or an effective parameter count for the model near a particular solution. And we've found that you can actually estimate it for real networks using sampling methods, and it tells you something. When a model undergoes a phase transition during training, say it learns a new circuit or a new kind of structure, you often see a signature in the learning coefficient. So it gives you a way to detect, from the outside, that something qualitatively changed in what the model is doing, without needing to know in advance what to look for.

That connects to interpretability because a lot of interpretability right now is quite bottom-up. You look for features, you look for circuits, and you build up a picture. SLT offers something more top-down. It says: here's what the geometry tells you about which directions in parameter space matter and which ones don't. Those degenerate directions are exactly the ones where the model has unused capacity or redundancy, and the non-degenerate ones are where the model is actually committing to some computation. In principle, that's a guide for where to look. We've started doing things like refining the learning coefficient to be data-dependent, so you can ask how much of the model's structure is being used for this particular subset of inputs, and that starts to look like a tool for decomposing the model into functional components.

For evaluations, I think the honest answer is that we're earlier. The vision would be something like: current evals are behavioral, you probe the model with inputs and look at outputs, and that has fundamental limits because the model might behave differently in situations you didn't test. What you'd want is some way to make claims about the model's internal structure that generalize beyond the test distribution. SLT is one of the few frameworks that actually connects structure in the weights to generalization behavior in a mathematically grounded way. So the hope is that you could eventually have developmental evals, where you're tracking the formation of structure over training and flagging when something concerning starts to crystallize, rather than only testing the finished artifact.

I want to be careful not to oversell it. A lot of this is still at the stage of toy models and smallish transformers. But I think the direction is right, because ultimately if you want to say anything rigorous about why a model generalizes the way it does, you have to engage with the geometry, and SLT is the theory that does that.

astra-6.text:
I think the hope is that singular learning theory gives us a language for connecting a model’s internal structure to its behavior during learning. And that could be useful both for understanding what a model has learned and for recognizing when that changes.

The starting point is that neural networks are singular statistical models. Different parameter settings can represent the same function, and there are regions where some parameters matter much more than others. So counting parameters doesn’t really tell you how complex the learned solution is. Singular learning theory gives you a more refined notion of complexity that takes that geometry into account.

For interpretability, one direction is to use that to study developmental transitions: points in training where the model acquires a new structure or a new way of solving a task. You could then bring other interpretability tools to bear on those points and ask what actually changed. The geometry alone doesn’t tell you, ‘This is an induction head,’ or, ‘This model is reasoning.’ You still need to establish that connection.

For evaluation, the prospect is that these measurements could complement behavioral tests. A benchmark tells you how a model performs on the examples you give it. We’d also like to understand how robust that performance is, and whether training is taking the model into a qualitatively different regime. I’d treat that as a research direction, though, rather than an established safety diagnostic. There’s a substantial gap between having a mathematical theory of learning and having a reliable measurement that tells you something safety-relevant about a large model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the promise is that singular learning theory gives us a way to connect the geometry of a model’s loss landscape to what it has actually learned. And that could be useful for both evaluation and interpretability, although I’d distinguish the mathematical foundations from what we can reliably do with current models.

One of the central ideas is that counting parameters is a pretty poor way to measure the complexity of a neural network. Different parameter settings can implement the same function, and there can be lots of directions in parameter space that don’t change the model’s behavior. Singular learning theory gives you quantities, like the learning coefficient, that are sensitive to that structure.

For interpretability, the hope is that changes in those quantities can help us identify transitions during training: places where the model starts organizing its computation differently. You could then use those transitions to guide more detailed investigation. Rather than looking at arbitrary checkpoints, you have a reason to ask, ‘What changed here? Did a new circuit form? Did the model acquire a different way of solving the task?’

For evaluation, I’m interested in whether that can give us information that behavioral tests alone miss. Two models might achieve similar scores while having learned quite different solutions. If we can characterize those differences, perhaps we can better understand when their behavior will generalize and when it will break down.

But a learning coefficient isn’t a safety score. There’s still a substantial gap between measuring something about the geometry and knowing what it means semantically. I see this as a potential foundation for better tools, to be used alongside behavioral evaluations and mechanistic interpretability, rather than something that replaces them.
